## Derivation of the Discrete-Time Tangency (Invariance) Condition

### Setup

Consider the discrete-time map $F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m$ defined by
$$F(x,y) = \bigl(f(x,y),\; g(x,y)\bigr),$$
and the candidate invariant manifold given as the graph
$$M = \bigl\{(x, h(x)) : x \in \mathbb{R}^n\bigr\}, \qquad h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m.$$

### Step 1 — Definition of Invariance

The manifold $M$ is **invariant** under $F$ if $F(M)\subseteq M$; that is, every point of $M$ is mapped back into $M$.

Take an arbitrary point $(x, y)\in M$, so $y = h(x)$. Its image under one iteration of the map is
$$F(x, h(x)) = \bigl(f(x, h(x)),\; g(x, h(x))\bigr).$$

For this image to lie in $M$, the second component must equal $h$ evaluated at the first component. This gives the **discrete-time tangency (invariance) condition**:

$$\boxed{\;g\bigl(x,\, h(x)\bigr) \;=\; h\!\left(f\bigl(x,\, h(x)\bigr)\right) \quad \text{for all } x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\;}$$

This is the exact discrete-time analogue of the continuous-time tangency condition $Dh(x)\,F(x,h(x)) = G(x,h(x))$. In continuous time, tangency means the vector field lies in the tangent space of the graph; in discrete time, the map sends points to points, so the analogue is the **functional equation** requiring that the image of every graph point is again a graph point.

### Step 2 — Geometric Interpretation

The tangent space to the graph $M$ at $(x, h(x))$ is
$$T_{(x,h(x))}M = \bigl\{(v,\, Dh(x)\,v) : v\in\mathbb{R}^n\bigr\}.$$

In continuous time, the vector field $(F, G)$ must lie in this tangent space, yielding $G = Dh\, F$. In discrete time there is no vector field to constrain; instead, the map $F$ must send the entire graph into itself, which is precisely the functional equation above. The "tangency" is therefore encoded not as a pointwise vector condition but as a **global functional relation** between $f$, $g$, and $h$.

### Step 3 — Linearized (Differentiated) Form

When $f$, $g$, and $h$ are $C^1$, we may differentiate the invariance condition with respect to $x$. Applying the chain rule to both sides of $g(x, h(x)) = h(f(x, h(x)))$:

$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\bigl(x,h(x)\bigr) \;+\; \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\bigl(x,h(x)\bigr)\,Dh(x) \;=\; Dh\!\left(f(x,h(x))\right)\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigl(x,h(x)\bigr) \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\bigl(x,h(x)\bigr)\,Dh(x)\right].$$

This is the **linearized invariance equation**. It governs how the Jacobian $Dh$ is transported under the dynamics and is the direct discrete-time counterpart of the continuous-time tangency condition $Dh\,F = G$. It states that the derivative of the map, restricted to the tangent bundle of $M$, maps tangent vectors of $M$ to tangent vectors of $M$—i.e., the linearized map preserves the tangent bundle of the graph.

### Step 4 — Differentiability Requirements

The differentiability requirements depend on how far one wishes to push the analysis:

| Requirement | Minimum regularity needed |
|---|---|
| **Functional equation** $g(x,h(x))=h(f(x,h(x)))$ well-defined | $f, g$ at least $C^0$ (continuous); $h$ at least $C^0$ |
| **Linearized invariance equation** (differentiated form) valid | $f, g \in C^1$ and $h \in C^1$ |
| **Persistence / normally hyperbolic invariant manifold theory** (Hadamard graph transform, Fenichel-type results for maps) | $f, g \in C^k$ with $k \geq 1$; $h$ inherits $C^k$ regularity under normal hyperbolicity |

**Summary of the minimal requirement:** For the tangency condition in its differentiated (linearized) form to hold—that is, for the derivative $Dh$ to satisfy the transported relation—the map $(f,g)$ and the function $h$ must each be **at least $C^1$** (continuously differentiable). The functional equation itself requires only continuity, but the tangency interpretation involving tangent spaces and the linearized dynamics on the manifold requires first derivatives to exist and be continuous.

For higher-order analysis—such as computing normal forms restricted to the invariant manifold, or establishing persistence of the manifold under perturbations via the graph transform—one requires $f, g \in C^k$ with $k\geq 1$ (commonly $k \geq 2$ for persistence theorems), and the invariant manifold function $h$ is then guaranteed to be of the same class $C^k$ provided the manifold is normally hyperbolic.
